tour.title: A quick tour of the map
transcript: One map of the world’s oil and gas infrastructure: 26 major pipelines, 64 oil and gas fields, 68 ports, refineries, LNG terminals and production sites, and 8 shipping chokepoints.
Benchmark prices run along the top, measured against the week before the crisis. Brent is at $99.7, up 38%.
Every dataset shows how fresh it is.
Switch layers on and off: pipelines, fields, refineries, LNG terminals, ports and chokepoints.
Rings mark assets that aren’t operating normally: closed, damaged, offline, disrupted or reduced. 17 are flagged right now.
Hide the panel whenever you want more room.
Jump straight to a region…
…and click any asset.
Yanbu Terminal: what it does, its current status and related developments, with sources and a confidence label for every claim.
The Latest tab is a daily, sourced feed of what’s changing, led by a summary of the situation.
Filter it by time window or category…
…and click an event to see where it happened.
Chokepoints shows daily tanker transits from IMF PortWatch satellite data, against the pre-crisis baseline. Counts lag about a week.
Click one for its full story: here, Strait of Hormuz.
Pump prices: weekly petrol and diesel prices for the US, every EU country and the UK, from official statistics.
US gasoline: 4.46 $/gal, up 52% since February.
Click any country for its price history.
Updated every day by a research agent, with a source behind every claim. Free, and no ads.

what-if.title: What if the Strait of Hormuz shut completely?
transcript: This map tracks the world’s oil and gas pipelines, export terminals and shipping chokepoints, with sourced daily updates.
Start by simplifying: switch off the layers this story doesn’t need, like gas pipelines, fields and recent events.
Then hide the panel to give the map more room.
In 2025 about 19.9 million barrels a day of oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz: roughly 19% of world demand.
The What-if tab lets you close any of six major chokepoints, alone or together.
Close Hormuz. Red dashes are tanker and LNG routes that are cut, and 24 terminals, refineries and other assets are left stranded.
Green lines are the only bypass routes the model counts: East-West Pipeline and Habshan–Fujairah Pipeline.
Net result: a 16.4 mb/d oil shortfall, 15.8% of world demand, even after 3.5 mb/d of pipeline bypass.
And 20% of global LNG trade has no way out at all.
IEA emergency stocks would cover that gap for about 73 days, if they could be released that fast. In practice, maximum release rates are far below a gap this size.
It also reads each facility’s live status. Right now East-West Pipeline is reduced and Yanbu Terminal and Fujairah are disrupted, so real bypass capacity is likely lower.
Most exposed: China, India and Japan & South Korea.
Closures combine. Add Bab el-Mandeb and Red Sea tankers divert around the Cape of Good Hope, about 12 extra days at sea.
What-if is an illustrative model of a total shutdown. The real strait’s status is tracked separately, with a source behind every claim.

daily-updates.title: How the map stays current and sourced
transcript: Every morning an automated research agent reviews independent reporting since its last run, then updates events, facility status and prices.
The Latest tab leads with the situation in a paragraph, dated Oct 1, 2026.
Need context? The background explains how we got here.
Below it, every development gets a date, a category, a severity colour and a confidence label, with links to its sources.
Confirmed means two or more independent sources. Reported, one reputable source. Unverified, a claim by a party to the conflict.
Those claims appear only when the claim itself is news: attributed by name, marked unverified, and never turned into facts or figures.
On the map, recent events pulse, coloured by severity.
Hover one for the headline…
…and click it to open the asset it affects.
Each asset keeps its own status note and history of related developments. This one was last verified Sep 28, 2026.
Every event is also archived, month by month…
…with the sources for each one, and an RSS feed to follow along.
One sourcing rule for every government that is party to a conflict: verify, then use. Ship traffic in contested waters comes only from independent trackers.
Routine updates publish automatically. Big changes, like a chokepoint changing status, wait for human review.
Significant developments are also posted to X and Bluesky, under the same rules.

embedding.title: Embed the live map on your site
transcript: Want the map in your own article, blog post or lesson? There’s a view made for that.
Add ?embed=1 to the address…
…and you get just the map: no panels, with a small link back to the full site.
Add &region= to choose where it opens: europe…
…mideast, asia or americas.
Then drop it into any page with an iframe.
It sits in your page like any other element…
…and readers can pan around it…
…and hover anything for details.
It stays current as the map updates every day. Free, with no ads, no cookies and no tracking across sites.
Get the code from the About page…
…pick where the map opens…
…and copy it in one click.
